unit.title: Develop and apply conversational skills in a foreign language

summary: This unit teaches you basic conversational Spanish for a salon or hotel spa: how to say words clearly, greet and address guests politely, take bookings, ask safety questions in a consultation, give instructions and check comfort during a service, talk about hair, nails and skin, handle prices and payment, say goodbye, and cope when you do not understand. It is Spanish for your work, not full fluency.

blocks.p: Jamaica welcomes visitors from many countries, and some of them speak Spanish: guests from Spain, Mexico, Colombia, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and other Spanish-speaking countries. A therapist or stylist who can greet a guest in her own language, ask the right safety questions and give simple instructions makes her feel welcome and keeps her safe. Spanish is also taught in Jamaican schools, so many trainees already know some words.

This unit is **conversational Spanish for the salon and spa**. You do not need to speak perfectly. You need a small set of correct, polite phrases, clear pronunciation, and the habit of checking that you and the guest understand each other. Where a word or phrase differs between countries, this kit gives the form that is understood almost everywhere in Latin America and Spain, and tells you when there is a difference.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks: a Spanish-English consultation card and a role play of a service visit, and a Spanish-English service menu with telephone bookings. In the practical tasks every member speaks Spanish. The assessor checks your accuracy, your politeness and whether you check that the guest has understood.

blocks.note: In practical work, practise the hands-on part only with a partner who agrees, using plain products. Photograph hands and the work area, not faces, unless the person agrees and the Centre allows it. Use made-up names and numbers.

sections.title: Why Spanish matters, and how to say it

ul: **Welcome and respect:** a guest who is greeted in Spanish feels welcome, relaxes and is more likely to return and recommend the salon.

**Safety:** before a colour, a wax, a facial or a massage you must ask about allergies, skin problems, medicines and pregnancy. If the guest cannot understand your questions, she cannot answer truthfully, and she could be burned or have a reaction.
**Fewer mistakes:** a guest who understands the length, the colour and the price you are offering is less likely to complain.
**Comfort checks:** you need to hear 'hot' or 'it hurts' and understand at once.
Learn **phrases**, not single words, and practise them aloud, a few each day.
Make a small phrase card for your station, with the Spanish and the English side by side.
Practise with a partner in the roles of stylist and guest.
Listen to Spanish songs, radio or videos, and notice how the phrases sound.
Do not be afraid of mistakes: guests are grateful for the effort. Always smile and speak slowly.

blocks.p: Spanish is written the way it is said, and has very regular sounds. The sounds below are those used in Latin America; in most of Spain, c before e or i and z sound like th in 'thin'.

head: Letter
Sound
Examples
rows: Five short, clear vowels: ah, eh, ee, oh, oo. Say each one the same way every time.
A strong h, from the back of the throat. Also g before e or i.
Like the y in 'yes' (in most of Latin America).
Like the y in 'yes' when it is at the start of a word.
Like k. The u is silent.
r is a quick tap; rr and r at the start of a word are rolled.

ul: An **accent mark** (á, é, í, ó, ú) shows which syllable is stressed. It is part of the spelling: copy it when you write a name or a word. Examples: champú, manicura, miércoles.
Without a mark, words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-last syllable (CI-ta, MA-no, LU-nes); other words are stressed on the last (se-ÑOR, es-PE-jo).
Some accents change the meaning: **sí** (yes) and **si** (if); **mañana** means both 'tomorrow' and 'morning'.
**¿ ?** and **¡ !** are written at the start and end of questions and exclamations: ¿Tiene cita? ¡Está muy caliente!
**ñ** is a separate letter of the Spanish alphabet. Do not replace ñ with n: 'una' (a) and 'uña' (nail) are different words.

head: Letters
Names
rows: A B C D E F G
a, be, ce, de, e, efe, ge
H I J K L M N Ñ
hache, i, jota, ka, ele, eme, ene, eñe
O P Q R S T U
o, pe, cu, erre, ese, te, u
uve (or ve), doble uve, equis, i griega, zeta

blocks.p: To ask a guest to spell her name, say: '¿Cómo se escribe su apellido?' (How do you write your surname?) or '¿Puede deletrearlo, por favor?' (Can you spell it, please?). Write it down as she says it and read it back.

ul: Every noun is **masculine** or **feminine**: el pelo, la uña. 'El' and 'la' mean 'the'; 'un' and 'una' mean 'a'. For more than one, use los and las: los pies, las manos.
Describing words agree: a woman is **alérgica**, **cómoda**, **embarazada**; a man is **alérgico**, **cómodo**. When you do not know, use the feminine for a woman and the masculine for a man.

To one adult you do not know, use **usted** (polite you), not **tú** (the friendly form kept for family, friends and children). With usted, the verb ends as for 'he' or 'she': ¿Tiene cita? ¿Paga con tarjeta?
To give a polite command to one person with usted, use the forms in the instruction tables below: Siéntese. Cierre los ojos. Add 'por favor'.

head: Spanish
English
When
rows: After dark; also to say good night.
Informal; follow it with the time-of-day greeting for a new guest.
Very well, thank you. And you?
Bienvenida to a woman, bienvenido to a man; bienvenidos to a group.

head: Spanish
English
rows: Thank you / Thank you very much
Excuse me (to pass or to get attention)

ul: Use **usted** and a title with the surname: **señora** (madam, Mrs.), **señor** (sir, Mr.) and **señorita** (a young woman or girl). For an adult woman, 'señora' is the safe choice.
Do not use the first name or friendly words such as 'amigo' or 'mi amor' until the guest invites you to. 'Tú' is used more in some countries than others, but 'usted' is never wrong for a new guest.

Many Spanish speakers have **two surnames**: the father's first, then the mother's. María López García is addressed as 'Señora López'. A woman usually keeps her own surnames when she marries. Check the spelling with her, and write it as she gives it, with the accents.
Examples: 'Buenos días, señora López.' 'Buenas tardes, señor Pérez.'

A handshake is the usual polite greeting. Some guests, especially from Spain and Latin America, greet with a light kiss on the cheek, one or two. Respond warmly and stay professional; do not start it yourself.
Look at the guest and smile. A warm, patient manner matters as much as correct grammar.
**Ask before you touch**: tell the guest what you are going to do and show it with your hands before you begin.
Be private and careful with questions such as pregnancy: ask quietly and only when it matters for safety.

Do not laugh at an accent or a word that is different from what you learnt. Words differ from country to country, for example the word for the fringe of the hair: flequillo (Spain), cerquillo, fleco and other words. Ask the guest to show you.
Be patient with yourself and with the guest. Speak slowly, not loudly, and smile.

blocks.note: Guests may come from many countries and cultures. Your Jamaican warmth is a strength. Follow the salon's rules about personal contact and photographs.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Numbers, days, times, prices and payment

head: Number
Spanish
rows: cien (before another number: ciento, as in ciento cinco = 105)

blocks.note: Do not mix up similar numbers: cuarenta (40) and cuatrocientos (400); quince (15) and cincuenta (50); seis (6) and siete (7). When the price matters, say the number and **write it down** for the guest, so she sees it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Spanish
English
Spanish
English
rows: en quince días / dentro de dos semanas

blocks.p: Days of the week are written with a small letter in Spanish. Use **el** before a day to mean 'on': el jueves (on Thursday), los sábados (on Saturdays). 'Por la mañana' is 'in the morning', 'por la tarde' 'in the afternoon', 'por la noche' 'at night'.

head: Spanish
Time
rows: a las diez de la mañana
a las cuatro de la tarde

blocks.p: Say 'a las' before the time in an appointment: 'una cita a las diez', 'una manicura a las cuatro y media'. For one o'clock use 'a la una'.

head: Spanish
English
rows: It costs six thousand two hundred dollars.
En total son doce mil quinientos dólares jamaicanos.
In total it is twelve thousand five hundred Jamaican dollars.
Will you pay by cash or card?
Aquí tiene la lista de precios.

ul: State the price in the same currency as the price list. If a guest wants to pay in another currency, follow the salon's own exchange rate and rules, and ask your supervisor. Never invent a rate.
Write the total on a piece of paper and show it to her, and show the price list on the desk. Check that she agrees to the price before she pays.
Count the change out loud, slowly, and put it in her hand.
Tips are the guest's choice. Follow the salon's policy: thank her with 'Muchas gracias.'

blocks.note: The Spanish word for 'Jamaican' is 'jamaicano' (some people also use 'jamaiquino'). A guest will understand either.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Before any service, you must find out whether it is safe for the guest. In Spanish you can do this with a set of short questions that she can answer 'sí' or 'no'. Always ask them in a private place, quietly, and write the answers on her record card.

head: Spanish
English
Why you ask
rows: ¿Qué desea hoy? / ¿Qué le gustaría hacerse hoy?
Colour, wax, creams and gloves can cause a reaction.
Are you allergic to any product?
Soy alérgica al látex. / Soy alérgico al níquel.
I am allergic to latex. / I am allergic to nickel.
Her answer: then use non-latex gloves, check the products, and write it down.
Have you had the allergy (skin) test?
Many colours need a skin test first; follow the maker's instructions.
Some medicines make the skin thin or sensitive.
Choose mild products and test first.
¿Tiene alguna herida, irritación o quemadura de sol?
Do you have any cut, irritation or sunburn?
Broken, sore or sunburnt skin must not be treated with many services.
Itching can mean a scalp problem or lice.
Some products and treatments are not suitable in pregnancy. Ask quietly and privately.
Do you have any health problem?
For example diabetes or heart problems matter for a pedicure, a wax or a massage.
Have you coloured your hair recently?
Past chemical services change what is safe today.
A first-time guest needs more explanation.

head: Spanish
English
rows: I have a cut or sore

blocks.h: What you do with her answers

ul: **Allergy to something in the service:** do not use it. Use a safe alternative, or do not give the service. Write it on her record.
**No skin test before a colour that needs one:** do not apply the colour. Do the test and book her for after the time the maker says (often 24 to 48 hours; follow the product's instructions).
**A cut, sore, rash, sunburn or infection in the area:** do not treat that area. Explain politely and offer another service or ask her to see a doctor. Do not say what you think the condition is.
**Pregnancy:** follow the product maker's instructions and your supervisor's advice; some products or treatments are not suitable.
**You do not understand her answers:** do not guess. Slow down, use yes/no questions and the form, ask a colleague, or offer a safer service.

blocks.note: Never start a chemical service, a wax or a body treatment when you are not sure that you understand the guest's answers about her health. A misunderstanding can cause a burn or an allergic reaction. If you cannot be sure, offer a safe alternative and record what happened.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Copy the guest's name exactly, with the accents and ñ, for example 'Jiménez' or 'Peña'. Write her allergies in English as well as Spanish so that any colleague can read them. Ask her to sign the card if the salon requires it, and keep it private.

sections.title: Instructions and comfort during the service

blocks.p: During a service you ask the guest to move, sit, lie, tilt her head or keep still. Use polite commands with **usted** and add 'por favor'. Show the movement with your hands, too. Check her comfort often and stop at once if she tells you something is wrong.

head: Spanish
English
Use
rows: Gire la cabeza a la derecha / a la izquierda.
Turn your head to the right / to the left.

blocks.note: The ending 'se' in 'siéntese', 'relájese' and 'levántese' means 'yourself'. It is attached to the end of the command. In a refusal it moves in front: 'No se mueva' (do not move). You do not need to study grammar, only to learn these as phrases.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Spanish
English
rows: ¿Está bien la presión? ¿Más fuerte o más suave?
Is the pressure all right? Harder or softer?
Are you cold? / Are you hot?

head: Spanish
English
What you do
rows: Stop at once; take the heat or product away; check the skin and the temperature.
Stop; ask where; check; do not continue until the cause is fixed and she agrees.
Stop; rinse the product off with cool or lukewarm running water; call the supervisor.
Stop; check for a reaction; call the supervisor.
I feel dizzy. / I feel unwell.
Stop; sit her up safely; give water; call the supervisor.
I am cold. / I am hot.
Adjust the fan, blanket or heat.

ul: **Test heat first.** Test water, wax and warm tools on the inside of your wrist before they touch the guest. Ask: '¿Está bien la temperatura?'

**First aid for a burn:** cool the area with cool running water, tell your supervisor, and apologise: 'Lo siento. Voy a enfriar la zona con agua fría.' (I am sorry. I am going to cool the area with cold water.) Write it in the accident record.
**Never ignore** 'me duele' or 'está muy caliente'. Even if you think the temperature is fine, stop and check.

blocks.h: Other ways to make yourself understood

head: Tool
How it helps
Example
rows: The guest points to what she wants, so you do not guess the length or style.
A photo of a hairstyle, nail design or brow shape.
'Rojo' for red; she points to the chart to be sure.
Avoids mistakes with prices and times.
Shows the length or the place.
Fingers to show how much to cut; point to the basin: 'Aquí, por favor.'
Helps with health questions and complaints.
'Un momento, voy a buscar a mi compañera.'
A phrase card or a translation app
Use it for single phrases; check the meaning with the guest.

ul: Always check back: '¿Así?' (Like this?) or '¿Es correcto?' (Is that right?) before you start.

A translation app helps with a word or a sentence, but it can make mistakes. Never rely on it alone for a health question before a chemical service. Do not type her full name, address or card number into an app, and keep her details private.
A friend or relative can help translate if the guest agrees, but keep health questions private if you can.
If you still cannot be sure, do not carry out a risky service. Offer a safe one and record what happened.

blocks.h: Practical task 1: consultation card and role play

ul: Make a Spanish-English consultation card with at least **20 phrases**, spelt correctly with accents, ñ, ¿ and ¡, grouped as: welcome and booking; consultation questions; instructions during the service; comfort checks; aftercare, payment and goodbye.

Act out a visit by a Spanish-speaking guest for one service (a shampoo and blow-dry, a manicure, a facial or a hand and arm massage), in four stages: welcome at the desk; consultation; the service with instructions and comfort checks; and aftercare, payment and goodbye.
Every member plays the stylist or therapist in at least one stage and speaks Spanish in it.
The assessor may give an answer that needs a follow-up question, such as 'Soy alérgica' (I am allergic): ask '¿A qué?' (To what?)
Use plain products only, with a partner who agrees. Clean and disinfect tools and use fresh towels for each partner.

head: Stage
Phrases to use
rows: Buenos días. Bienvenida al salón. ¿Tiene cita? ¿Su nombre, por favor? Siéntese, por favor.
¿Tiene alguna alergia? ¿Toma algún medicamento? ¿Tiene la piel sensible? ¿Se hizo la prueba de alergia?
Siéntese aquí. Incline la cabeza hacia atrás. ¿Está bien el agua? ¿Le duele? No se mueva, por favor.
¿Le gusta? Use protector solar. Son nueve mil trescientos dólares. ¿Paga en efectivo o con tarjeta? Gracias por su visita. Hasta la próxima.

blocks.h: Practical task 2: service menu and telephone bookings

ul: Make a menu in Spanish and English with **at least eight services**, each with the Spanish name, the English name, the time it takes and the price in J$ (the assessor gives the prices or the group uses the Centre's price list). Add opening days and hours in Spanish.

Act out telephone bookings. Each member takes at least one call in Spanish: greet, find out the service, agree the day and time, take and spell the name and a phone number, write it on the booking sheet, repeat the details back and say goodbye. One call must be a change of booking to another day.
Use made-up names and numbers. Keep booking sheets private.

blocks.p: Opening days and hours, in Spanish: 'Abierto de lunes a sábado, de nueve a cinco.' (Open Monday to Saturday, from nine to five.) 'Cerrado los domingos.' (Closed on Sundays.)

blocks.note: Take short breaks if you work on a screen or a poster for a long time. Keep walkways clear and use only made-up details.

c1.title: A manicure for a guest from Madrid, in Negril
c1.text: At a hotel spa in Negril, trainee Kimberly meets Sra. Carmen Ruiz Torres, a guest from Madrid. It is three in the afternoon. The guest says: 'Buenas tardes. Tengo una reserva a las cinco menos cuarto. Tengo la piel muy sensible y soy alérgica a algunos esmaltes.'

c2.title: A telephone booking in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Receptionist Odalie answers the phone at a salon in Ocho Rios. A caller says: 'Quisiera una cita para un masaje de espalda el viernes a las dos.' Odalie checks the book and finds the time is free. The price on the list for the massage is J$6,200. When she asks for the caller's surname, the caller spells it: 'ge, o, eme, e, zeta.'

c3.title: Before a colour in Montego Bay
c3.text: Trainee Tamara is about to colour the hair of Sra. Valentina Rojas, a guest from Bogotá, at a salon in Montego Bay. During the consultation, the guest says: 'Me pica la cabeza y tengo una herida pequeña detrás de la oreja.' Later, when Tamara is rinsing the colour at the basin, the guest says: '¡Me arde mucho!'

c4.title: A haircut at the Centre's training salon
c4.text: At the Centre's training salon in Kingston, a visitor from the Dominican Republic, Sr. Rafael Peña, asks for a haircut. He says: 'Quiero cortarme dos dedos, no más.' The trainee wants him to tilt his head forward so that she can cut the nape. When she has finished, she holds up a hand mirror to check that he is happy.

c5.title: Paying and leaving, in Mandeville
c5.text: At a salon in Mandeville, a guest from Cuba, Sra. Dayana Ortiz, has had a facial and a manicure. The receptionist says: 'En total son nueve mil trescientos dólares jamaicanos.' The guest answers: 'No tengo efectivo. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?' As she leaves, the therapist tells her: 'Beba mucha agua. Gracias por su visita. Hasta la próxima.'

c6.title: A guest who speaks fast, in Portmore
c6.text: A Spanish-speaking guest at a salon in Portmore speaks very quickly to trainee Shanice, who understands only a few words. Shanice wants to ask her to say it again, tell her that she speaks only a little Spanish, ask her to point to a photo of the style she wants, and then go to find a Spanish-speaking colleague.

questions.q: Which greeting should Kimberly use at this time of day?
questions.why: 'Buenas tardes' is used from about noon until dusk. 'Buenos días' is for the morning, 'buenas noches' for after dark, and 'hasta luego' is a goodbye.

questions.q: What time is the guest's booking, 'a las cinco menos cuarto'?
questions.why: 'Menos cuarto' means a quarter to the hour, so 'las cinco menos cuarto' is 4:45. 'Y cuarto' would be a quarter past.

questions.q: What should Kimberly do after hearing that the guest is allergic to some nail polishes?
o: Ask which products cause it, use safe ones or test first, and record it
Use the polish she likes best, and quickly wash her hands if she reacts
Ask her to bring her own polish tomorrow, and book her for the same time
Carry on, as polish only touches the nails and cannot affect the skin
questions.why: Find out what she reacts to, use a safe alternative or test first as the maker says, and record it. Polish can touch the skin around the nails and cause a reaction.

questions.q: When does the caller want her massage?
questions.why: 'El viernes' is Friday and 'a las dos' is at two o'clock. 'Jueves' is Thursday and 'martes' is Tuesday.

questions.q: The caller asks '¿Cuánto cuesta?' Which sentence gives the price of J$6,200?
questions.why: 6,000 is 'seis mil' and 200 is 'doscientos', so 6,200 is 'seis mil doscientos'. 'Seiscientos' is 600, 'sesenta y dos' is 62.

questions.q: How is the surname that the caller spelled, 'ge, o, eme, e, zeta', written?
questions.why: 'Ge' is G, 'o' is O, 'eme' is M, 'e' is E and 'zeta' is Z, so the name is GOMEZ. Always write it down and read it back to check.

questions.q: What is the guest telling Tamara in the consultation?
o: Her head hurts and she has a headache after the sun
Her head itches and she has a small wound behind her ear
She has a cut on her hand and her scalp feels cold
She has coloured her hair recently and her ear itches
questions.why: 'Me pica la cabeza' means 'my head itches' and 'tengo una herida pequeña detrás de la oreja' means 'I have a small cut or wound behind the ear'.

questions.q: What is the safest thing for Tamara to do before the colour?
o: Colour all of her hair except the area behind the ear
Put a plaster over the wound and then colour the hair as planned
Do not colour; explain politely and suggest she sees a doctor
Use half the colour mixture so that the skin is less affected
questions.why: Colour on a wound or an itching, possibly infected scalp can burn or cause a reaction. Do not apply it, explain politely without naming a condition, suggest a doctor and offer something safe.

questions.q: While rinsing, the guest says '¡Me arde mucho!' What should Tamara do first?
o: Keep rinsing quickly, as the colour is almost finished anyway
Tell her this feeling is normal and ask her to wait until the end
Stop, rinse the colour off with lukewarm water, and call the supervisor
Ask her to repeat the sentence slowly, then carry on with the rinse
questions.why: 'Me arde' means 'it burns'. A burning scalp is a warning: stop at once, remove the product with cool or lukewarm running water, check the skin and call the supervisor.

questions.q: What does Sr. Peña want?
o: Two centimetres cut from every part of the hair
Only two fingers' width cut, and no more
A cut that is two fingers shorter than before at the back
To have his hair cut twice in two days
questions.why: 'Quiero cortarme dos dedos, no más' means 'I want two fingers cut, no more'. Hold up your fingers and ask '¿Así?' to check you understand.

questions.q: Which phrase asks him to tilt his head forward?
o: Incline la cabeza hacia adelante, por favor
Incline la cabeza hacia atrás, por favor
Gire la cabeza a la derecha, por favor
questions.why: 'Hacia adelante' means 'forward'. 'Hacia atrás' is backward, 'gire a la derecha' is turn to the right, and 'levante la barbilla' is lift your chin.

questions.q: The trainee holds up the mirror and asks, '¿Así está bien?' What is she asking?
o: Is it all right like this?
questions.why: '¿Así está bien?' means 'Is it all right like this?' It lets the client say if she wants a change before she leaves.

questions.q: How much is the guest's total in J$?
questions.why: 'Nueve mil' is 9,000 and 'trescientos' is 300, so 'nueve mil trescientos' is 9,300.

questions.q: What is the guest asking when she says, 'No tengo efectivo. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?'
o: She has no cash and asks if she can pay by card
She has no money and asks for a discount
She has lost her card and asks to pay tomorrow
She wants a receipt and asks to pay with cash
questions.why: 'No tengo efectivo' means 'I have no cash' and 'con tarjeta' means 'by card'. Check the salon's rules and say yes or no politely.

questions.q: What is the therapist's aftercare advice, 'Beba mucha agua'?
questions.why: 'Beba' means 'drink' (the polite command) and 'mucha agua' means 'plenty of water'.

questions.q: Which phrase asks the guest to say it again?
questions.why: 'Repetir' means 'to repeat'. 'Pagar' is to pay, 'esperar' is to wait and 'firmar' is to sign.

questions.q: Which sentence tells the guest that Shanice speaks only a little Spanish?
questions.why: 'Hablo un poco de español' means 'I speak a little Spanish'. It sets the guest's expectation and she will usually slow down.

questions.q: Shanice says, 'Un momento, por favor. Voy a buscar a mi compañera.' What does this mean?
o: Wait here. I am going to pay my colleague.
One moment. I am going to find my colleague.
Come back later. My colleague is not here.
One moment. I am going to call the guest's friend.
questions.why: 'Un momento, por favor' means 'one moment, please' and 'voy a buscar a mi compañera' means 'I am going to find my colleague'.

questions.q: How is 'll' said in 'llamo' in most of Latin America?
questions.why: In most of Latin America 'll' sounds like the y in 'yes', so 'llamo' is said 'YA-mo'. Remember that 'h' is silent and 'j' is a strong 'h'.

questions.q: A man comes in. Which word welcomes him to the salon?
questions.why: 'Bienvenido' is for one man, 'bienvenida' for one woman, and 'bienvenidos' for a group. Words that describe people match their gender.
